questions.q: Define imagery and metaphor in your own words, giving one example of each from the opening paragraph of *Eveline*.
questions.a: Imagery: “odour of dusty cretonne” (olfactory + tactile). Metaphor: “evening invade the avenue” (evening is implicitly compared to an invading army). A wrong answer that says “imagery is just description” misses the sensory specificity; a wrong answer that calls “evening invade” a simile misses the absence of “like/as.”

questions.q: Explain the difference between literal imagery and metaphorical imagery. Using the phrase “her head was leaned against the window curtains,” say whether it is literal or metaphorical and why.
questions.a: Literal imagery describes a physical action exactly as it happens — Eveline’s head really rests on the curtain. Metaphorical imagery would be “her head was a stone against the window.” The given phrase is literal. A student who labels it metaphorical confuses *any* descriptive language with figurative language.

questions.q: Identify one example of auditory imagery and one of kinesthetic (movement) imagery from the middle section of the story (after Eveline reviews the familiar objects). Quote the phrase and name the sense.
questions.a: Auditory: “a street organ playing” (hearing). Kinesthetic: “she elbowed her way through the crowds” (bodily movement). A wrong answer that picks “the boat blew a long mournful whistle” for the middle section shows inability to locate textual segments.

questions.q: Compare the metaphorical function of the “window” in the first paragraph with the “iron railing” in the final scene. How does each act as a metaphor for Eveline’s psychological state?
questions.a: The window is a transparent barrier — she sees the world but cannot join it; it frames her passivity. The iron railing is a cold, hard grip she *chooses* to clutch — it transforms the barrier into an active anchor preventing escape. A student who says “both are just objects” fails to see the shift from passive framing to active self-entrapment.

questions.q: Evaluate which metaphor — “evening invade the avenue,” “all the seas of the world tumbled about her heart,” or “like a helpless animal” — most powerfully conveys the theme of paralysis. Justify your choice with two reasons.
questions.a: “All the seas of the world tumbled about her heart” is strongest because (1) the hyperbole “all the seas” magnifies internal chaos to a cosmic scale, and (2) the verb “tumbled” mimics the physical sensation of drowning, making paralysis visceral. A student who picks “like a helpless animal” and calls it a metaphor (it’s a simile) reveals confusion between device categories.

questions.q: Write a four-sentence paragraph describing a student frozen before an exam hall door, using at least two sensory images and one original metaphor (not from *Eveline*) to convey paralysis.
questions.a: Example: “The corridor smelled of floor wax and anxiety (olfactory). His fingers, cold as iron filings (metaphor), gripped the admit card until the edges frayed (tactile). The bell rang, a hammer striking glass (auditory + metaphor), but his feet had grown roots into the linoleum (metaphor).” A poor answer uses only visual details or clichéd metaphors (“heart pounded like a drum”), showing inability to transfer the skill.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagery is the use of vivid, sensory language that appeals to the five senses (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste) to create concrete mental pictures and physical ______ for the reader.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are sitting in the exam hall and the question reads: “How does Joyce use the image of ‘dusty cretonne’ and the metaphor of the sea to reveal Eveline’s ______ to leave?” You freeze because you remember the words but not *how* they work.
What is Imagery? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Imagery is the use of vivid, sensory language that appeals to the five senses (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste) to create concrete mental pictures and physical sensations for the reader.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Imagery?
questions.a: Students treat imagery and metaphor as *identification exercises* — “spot the device, name it, move on.” They write “Joyce uses olfactory imagery: ‘odour of dusty cretonne’” and stop, thinking the job is done.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to (1) identify specific instances of visual, olfactory, tactile, auditory, and kinesthetic imagery in the story, (2) distinguish between literal description and metaphorical language, (3) explain how each device contributes to characterisation, atmosphere, and the central theme of paralysis versus escape, and.
